A turnkey is something — a product, a property, a business, or a system — that is completely finished and fully ready to use the moment it is handed over, with no additional work required from the person receiving it.

The name captures this idea well: everything is already done for you, and all you have to do is "turn the key" — like turning a key to start a car, or turning a key to open the door of a brand-new home. The instant you turn it, everything works.

The defining characteristic is that it is delivered in a finished, operational state. The provider has handled everything — the planning, the building, the setup, the testing — and the buyer inherits a complete, working thing.

This is the opposite of receiving something in an incomplete or raw state, where the buyer still has to do significant work before it's usable.

Real estate
A turnkey property (or simply "a turnkey") is a home that has been fully renovated — fresh paint, new flooring, repaired fixtures, working appliances — so the buyer can move in on the same day they purchase it. There's nothing to fix, nothing to upgrade. It's ready.

Compare this to buying a fixer-upper, where you spend months and significant money making the home livable before you can actually live in it. A fixer-upper is the opposite of a turnkey.

Business
A turnkey business is one that is already running — with employees hired, systems in place, customers established, and money coming in. The new owner simply steps in and takes over. There's no building from scratch.

Franchises are a classic example. When you buy a McDonald's franchise, the franchisor gives you the brand, the recipes, the equipment specifications, the training system, the supplier relationships, and the operational playbook. You receive a business that's ready to open. That's a turnkey.

Construction
In a turnkey contract, a construction company takes full responsibility for a building project — everything from the initial design to the final coat of paint — and hands the client a completed, move-in-ready structure at the end. The client doesn't have to manage architects, contractors, suppliers, or permits. They just receive the finished building.

Technology
A turnkey system is software or hardware that arrives pre-installed, pre-configured, and tested. The user doesn't have to set anything up. They just plug it in (or log in) and start working.
A Concrete Example to Make It Click

Suppose you want to open a coffee shop.

Option A (not a turnkey): You rent an empty commercial space. You then separately hire a designer, purchase espresso machines, build counters, install plumbing, source coffee beans, hire and train staff, set up a point-of-sale system, get the required permits, and build a website. After months of effort and coordination, the shop is finally ready to open.

Option B (a turnkey): You buy a package where someone hands you a fully equipped coffee shop — machines installed, counters built, staff trained, permits secured, POS system running, supplier agreements in place. On Day 1, you just show up, turn the key, and open the doors to customers.

Option B is a turnkey. All the complex, time-consuming work has already been done by someone else. Your involvement begins only at the finish line.

When something is called a turnkey, it signals:

  • Zero setup effort on the buyer's part
  • Complete delivery — nothing is missing or unfinished
  • Immediate usability — it works from the moment of handover
  • The provider bears all the complexity — the buyer doesn't need expertise, tools, or extra resources to get started

This is why turnkeys are attractive. They save time, reduce risk, and eliminate the need for the buyer to become an expert in something outside their core focus. A business owner who wants a coffee shop doesn't necessarily want to become an expert in construction, plumbing, and equipment installation. A turnkey spares them all of that.
An Important Nuance: Turnkey as a Selling Point

"Turnkey" is frequently used as a marketing and sales term. When a property, business, or system is advertised as a "turnkey," the seller is essentially promising: this is hassle-free and ready to go.

In practice, this means buyers should still do their homework. Not every seller's definition of "ready to use" meets the same standard. Some sellers loosely call something a turnkey when it still has gaps or hidden problems. So while the word signals completeness and readiness, a careful buyer will verify what exactly is included — and in what condition.

The word is a promise. Whether the promise holds depends on the specific deal.

In older English, a turnkey referred to a jailer — a prison guard whose specific job was to literally turn the large iron keys that locked and unlocked prison cell doors. This was a real occupational title in the 18th and 19th centuries.

This meaning is essentially obsolete today. You're very unlikely to encounter it in any modern text. In virtually every modern context — in business, real estate, technology, and construction — "turnkey" means the complete-and-ready-to-use concept described above.

A turnkey is something completely built, set up, and ready for immediate use, requiring nothing further from the recipient. The provider does all the work; the buyer just starts. It's the idea of maximum completeness and minimum friction — everything done, delivered, and functional, right from the first moment.
